item.title: Salahuddin: Don’t play Hasina card while seeking ties with Dhaka
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Saturday cautioned India against what he described as playing the “Hasina card” while claiming to seek friendly relations with Bangladesh, saying the two positions could not coexist.
“On the one hand, you say you want friendship with Bangladesh, and on the other, you play the Hasina card. These two things cannot go together,” Ahmed said.
He was speaking at a discussion titled “Teachers’ Role in the Fall of the Fascist Government” at Dhaka University’s Senate Bhaban, organized by Sada Dal, the BNP-backed teachers’ platform at the university, and the University Teachers’ Association of Bangladesh (UTAB).
The home minister referred to the United Nations’ findings on the July-August 2024 crackdown, saying more than 1,400 people were killed during the violence.
He also said the 2024 mass uprising was not, strictly speaking, a “revolution,” but a democratic movement led by the Students Against Discrimination platform to reclaim political and constitutional rights that had been stripped away under the previous Awami League government.
“A genuine revolution requires structural changes to the social and economic system,” he said, adding that this was not what Bangladeshis had fought for.
According to Salahuddin, people took to the streets demanding the restoration of their voting rights and democratic and constitutional freedoms.
He said the movement’s objective was therefore to restore those rights rather than bring about a revolutionary overhaul of the state.
The minister also outlined several constitutional reforms that he said the BNP would pursue, including limiting a prime minister’s tenure to 10 years, introducing direct election of the president by members of parliament, and establishing checks and balances between an upper and lower house of parliament.
Also speaking at the event, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, the prime minister’s adviser on political affairs, questioned how former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who is currently in India, was able to address a press conference in Delhi without government clearance.
He contrasted this with the treatment of Lord Carlile, a British lawyer who had sought to visit Dhaka in connection with the legal case involving Khaleda Zia.
Rizvi also referred to a recent art exhibition held at the residence of the Jamaat-e-Islami ameer, saying it did not include any image or reference to the person who declared Bangladesh’s independence.
Professor Morshed Hasan Khan, convener of Sada Dal, presided over the session, while its member secretary, Professor Mohammad Mohiuddin, moderated it.
Teachers from 26 public universities across the country attended the programme.

item.title: Tonu murder case: Ex-army personnel Hafizur sent to jail after bail stay
item.description:
Retired army personnel Hafizur Rahman was sent to jail on Saturday after being arrested following a stay on his High Court bail in the much-discussed Sohagi Jahan Tonu murder case in Comilla.
The Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) arrested Hafizur from his residence in Keraniganj, Dhaka, and produced him before Comilla Senior Judicial Magistrate Court-5.
Judge Tayeb Uddin subsequently ordered that he be sent to jail.
PBI Inspector and also the case's investigation officer Tarikul Islam confirmed the matter.
He said Hafizur was arrested to prevent him from fleeing and to comply with an order from the Appellate Division's chamber court.
Hafizur was released from Comilla Central Jail on August 4 after the High Court granted him bail on August 2. The state subsequently filed a leave-to-appeal petition seeking a stay on the bail order.
On August 6, Appellate Division Chamber Judge Justice Md Rezaul Haque stayed the High Court's bail order until August 9 and directed Hafizur to surrender within 24 hours. The court also ordered law enforcement agencies to arrest him if he failed to comply.
Hafizur did not surrender by the Friday evening deadline, according to Comilla Court Police Inspector Sadequr Rahman and Comilla Central Jail Senior Jail Superintendent Shah Alam Khan.
Sohagi Jahan Tonu, a history student at Comilla Victoria Government College and a theatre activist, went missing on March 20, 2016, while going to a private tutoring session inside Comilla Cantonment.
Her battered body was recovered from a bush near the cantonment's power house later that night.
The following day, her father Iyar Hossain filed a murder case with Kotwali Model Police Station against unidentified people.
During the investigation, the PBI first arrested Hafizur from Keraniganj on the night of April 21.

item.title: Journalist 'assaulted' in police van after filming police beating woman
item.description:
A multimedia reporter for Global Television, Bulbul Hossain, has alleged that police officers assaulted him inside a police van after he filmed them allegedly beating a woman in the capital’s Bijoy Sarani area.
Bulbul has submitted a written complaint to the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) commissioner, seeking legal and departmental action against the officers involved.
He submitted the complaint at the DMP headquarters in Ramna on Thursday afternoon.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Saturday, Bulbul said the incident occurred around 5:30pm on August 4 while he was on his way to cover a clash between Islami Chhatra Shibir and BNP activists.
He said that a police van was stuck in traffic near the Bijoy Sarani intersection, with several motorcycles blocking its path. Police officers reportedly got into arguments with some motorcyclists.
At one point, when a woman approached the van, several officers allegedly assaulted her. Bulbul said he began recording the incident in the line of his professional duty. The officers order him to delete the footage.
He alleged that the officers then forcibly took him into the police van and assaulted him after he refused to delete the video despite identifying himself as a journalist.
According to his complaint, the officers repeatedly struck him on the head, threw him to the floor of the van and beat him. He also alleged that one officer pressed a boot against his chest and attempted to suffocate him.
Bulbul said he was eventually able to leave the van after people nearby came forward upon hearing his screams.
He was later taken to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where doctors reportedly found injuries to his head, eye and chest and advised him to take three days of complete rest.
“I have filed a complaint with the DMP. I have been called by Tejgaon Police Station,” Bulbul said.
When contacted, Mahbubur Rahman, officer-in-charge of Tejgaon Industrial Area Police Station, told the Dhaka Tribune that he had not yet been informed about the complaint by the DMP.
“If the complainant brings a copy of the complaint submitted to the DMP commissioner, we will investigate the matter and take appropriate action,” he said.
In his complaint, Bulbul described the alleged assault as an attempt to silence independent journalism and a violation of human rights. He urged the authorities to identify the officers involved using video footage and eyewitness accounts and take legal and departmental action against them.

item.title: Speakers: Bangladesh needs action, not more environmental policies
item.description:
Bangladesh needs to move beyond environmental policies and commitments and focus on effective implementation, speakers said at a climate and nature conservation event at BRAC University on Saturday.
The remarks came at the two-day “Celebrating World Environment and Nature Conservation Day 2026” at the BRAC University auditorium, where government officials, academics, environmental experts, private-sector representatives, development practitioners and young people gathered to discuss practical solutions for protecting the country’s environment.
They stressed stronger institutions, practical solutions and collective action to address the country’s growing environmental challenges.
State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shaikh Faridul Islam speaking as the chief guest, said environmental protection requires more than policies and awareness, calling for practical and implementable solutions.
He highlighted government priorities including tree planting, coastal afforestation, carbon credits, plastic pollution, waste management, renewable energy, river and wetland restoration, recovery of forest land and pollution control.
The state minister said tree-planting targets should not be measured only by numbers, as species selection must take into account the ecological characteristics of different regions and adequate maintenance is essential for survival.
He also highlighted plans to plant 20 million keora trees in selected coastal areas and ongoing efforts to develop Bangladesh’s carbon-credit framework.
On plastic pollution, Faridul called for reducing unnecessary single-use polythene while ensuring practical alternatives for consumers and traders.
He also urged corporate organizations to use their corporate social responsibility funds strategically to support environmentally friendly alternatives.
Dr Ainun Nishat, professor emeritus and adviser to the Centre for Climate Change and Environmental Research (C3ER), said Bangladesh already has numerous laws, policies, strategies and international commitments on environmental protection.
“The question is not whether we understand the problem anymore. The question is whether we are willing to do enough about it,” he said.
Nishat called for stronger partnerships among the government, academia, private sector and other stakeholders.
He also said afforestation programs should not be judged solely by the number of trees planted, stressing the importance of selecting suitable species and ensuring their survival.
Dr A Atiq Rahman, executive director of the Bangladesh Centre for Advanced Studies, said climate action also requires strong institutions capable of implementing national plans.
“Institutional execution is essential. Action plans can only be successfully implemented when dedicated institutions have the capacity and responsibility to carry them forward,” he said.
Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director and CEO of Mutual Trust Bank PLC, said environmental protection should not be viewed solely as an environmental issue, as nature, society and the economy are closely interconnected.
The remarks came at the two-day “Celebrating World Environment and Nature Conservation Day 2026,” organized by C3ER at BRAC University with support from Mutual Trust Bank.
The program, being held on August 8-9, brings together government officials, academics, environmental experts, private-sector representatives, development practitioners and young people.
BRAC University Vice-Chancellor Professor Syed Ferhat Anwar said universities have a key role in generating locally relevant solutions and ensuring that research reaches communities beyond academic institutions.
The program continues Sunday with panel discussions, an Environmental Carnival, youth-focused climate sessions, exhibitions and knowledge-sharing activities.

item.title: Arsenal sign Brazil midfielder Guimaraes from Newcastle
item.description:
Premier League champions Arsenal have completed the signing of Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes for a reported fee of £75 million ($101.2 million), the two clubs announced Saturday.
The Brazil international, who spent four-and-a-half seasons with Newcastle, has signed a "long-term contract" with the Gunners, who ended a 22-year wait for a top-flight English league title last season.
The 28-year-old Guimaraes is Arsenal's most high-profile signing of the transfer window so far, joining fellow new arrivals Illan Meslier and Christos Tzolis at the Emirates Stadium.
"With Bruno joining us, we are further strengthening the heart of our team," said Arsenal sporting director Andrea Berta.
"As we have all seen, Bruno can play as a defensive midfielder and as a box-to-box player. He combines quality with quantity, and has provided goals and assists for his team every year.
"Bruno will allow Mikel (Arteta) to further develop our playing style and will also increase our internal competitiveness, which is essential for maintaining the standards required when we are aiming to win major trophies."
The transfer fee for Guimaraes was undisclosed, although Newcastle confirmed it was "one of the top 10 highest transfer fees ever received for a player aged 28 or over".
Guimaraes was also linked with Arsenal in January 2022, when he ended up leaving Lyon for Newcastle.
Now he finally does join up with Gunners boss Mikel Arteta in north London, after scoring 31 goals in 195 appearances for the Magpies.
Under coach Eddie Howe, Guimaraes helped Newcastle end a 54-year major trophy drought when they won the 2023 League Cup.
"This is one of the toughest decisions of my life. When I arrived, the club was in a challenging position and I am incredibly proud of what we achieved together," Guimaraes said in Newcastle's statement.
"I fell in love with this place. I really mean that."
Howe stepped down as Newcastle manager last week and has since been replaced by German Matthias Jaissle.
Guimaraes, who played for Brazil at the recent World Cup, will compete for a place in Arsenal's midfield with Declan Rice, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino.
Arsenal kick off their season against Manchester City in the Community Shield next Sunday, before starting their title defence against newly-promoted Coventry five days later.
Newcastle get their campaign under way against Liverpool at St James' Park on August 23.

item.title: FIFA chief Infantino gets backing of South American football
item.description:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino on Friday received support from several leading South American football figures as he visited Colombia amidst the crisis engulfing world football's governing body.
Infantino arrived early on Friday in the Colombian city of Cali to attend hard-right president Abelardo de la Espriella's inauguration.
Photos released by the Colombian Football Federation show a smiling Infantino standing alongside South American Football Confederation (CONMEBOL) president Alejandro Dominguez and the president of the Colombian federation, Ramon Jesurun.
The visit to Colombia comes as the head of world football has been embroiled in a storm following a much-criticised and ultimately abandoned plan to open the World Cup to private investment.
The 56-year-old Italian-Swiss lawyer, who has been in office since 2016, declined to answer a question from an AFP journalist about whether he considered FIFA's woes to be over.
Later, while attending a children's soccer festival at a sports complex in Cali, he spoke of his "happiness" at being at the event.
"It is a joy to be here today," the FIFA boss told dozens of children kitted out in football gear at an event in the southwestern city.
"Football is joy, football is happiness, football is unity," he said, adding that "so many champions" were born "in this part of the world, in this part of Colombia."
- 'Not necessary to always agree' -
Infantino, who will seek a fourth and final term in the presidential election in Rabat next March, is facing criticism, notably from European body UEFA, which on Thursday maintained its threat to boycott the World Cup despite FIFA's withdrawal of the private investment proposal.
CONMEBOL, which has only 10 FIFA-affiliated members but includes iconic federations such as Argentina and Brazil, had on Thursday expressed its "concern regarding the repeated unilateral actions taken" by FIFA.
However, when asked by a Colombian media outlet on Friday, the CONMEBOL president stated that "one cannot ignore the great work" done by Infantino.
"We must continue working for football through dialogue; it is not necessary to always agree," Dominguez added.
Following the powerful Argentine Football Association (AFA) and the Paraguayan federation on Thursday, Infantino also received support on Friday from two other South American federations -- Venezuela and Ecuador.
In line with their confederation's statement, they welcomed the withdrawal of the controversial plan to create a commercial entity open to private investors known as the FIFA Forward Enterprise.
In a letter to the FIFA chief, Ecuadorian federation president Francisco Egas Larreategui added that he had confidence in Infantino "as well as in those currently leading football to continue working for the good of our sport".
Close to figures on the right of politics, such as US President Donald Trump, Infantino attended De la Espriella's presidential inauguration ceremony later on Friday.
Colombia's incoming leader has broken with tradition by choosing to hold the ceremony in Cali, considered the capital of salsa, rather than before Congress in Bogota.

item.title: Maradona's 'Hand of God' ball heads to US auction
item.description:
The soccer ball that Diego Maradona used to score his infamous "Hand of God" goal during Argentina's win over England in the 1986 World Cup is expected to sell for $10 million at a US auction this month.
Maradona's goal in the quarter-final match at the Estadio Azteca saw him punch the ball past the England goalkeeper, with the South Americans ultimately winning 2-1.
After the game, the Argentine star said his goal was scored "a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God." His nation went on to win the World Cup.
Heritage Auctions, based in Texas, expects the ball will sell for eight figures when it goes under the hammer from August 21 to 23, with a $2.5 million opening bid.
"I think it's easily the most historic ball in the realm of soccer," Dan Imler, vice president of sports at Heritage Auctions, told AFP.
He noted it is also the ball that Maradona used, in the same match, to score the so-called "Goal of the Century" in which he dribbled past several English defenders before finishing past the goalkeeper.
"Both of the goals scored are just so iconic, so memorable," Imler said.
The jersey that Maradona, who died in November 2020, wore during the Argentina-England clash currently holds the record for the most expensive soccer shirt -- standing at $9.3 million.
Tensions between old foes Argentina and England flared again in a semi-final at this year's World Cup, where the South American side prevailed before losing the final.
Politically, the two sides have a long-standing sovereignty dispute over the Falkland Islands.

item.title: Travis Head wins Australian cricketer of the year award
item.description:
Star batsman Travis Head has won Australia's top cricketing honour for the second year in a row, edging Alex Carey to claim the Allan Border Medal.
The opener polled 153 votes, one ahead of wicketkeeper and South Australia teammate Carey, and three clear of fast bowler Mitchell Starc.
Fellow players, the media and umpires select the player of the year, with the awards handed out at a function in Brisbane on Friday evening.
Head played 30 matches across all three formats during the 2025-26 international season, blasting 1,437 runs.
The left-hander's highlight was a brilliant 123 off 83 balls on day two of the Ashes Test against England in Perth which helped Australia claim an eight-wicket win.
He went on to score two more big Ashes centuries.
"To think that I've got two medals and my kids can look at them and I can tell them (about it) in 20 years' time is pretty cool," said Head.
Head was only the fifth player to win back-to-back Allan Border Medals, following in the footsteps of Ricky Ponting, Michael Clarke, David Warner and Shane Watson.
Starc's remarkable durability through Australia's 11 Tests last season, including 31 Ashes wickets, saw him recognised as Australian Test player of the year.
Mitchell Marsh was named ODI player of the year while Tim David took the Twenty20 honour.
Earlier this year, Annabel Sutherland claimed her second consecutive Belinda Clark Award, which recognises Australia's best woman cricketer.

item.title: Eight films that ask more of you than most
item.description:
Most watchlists circulate the same twenty titles dressed up in new orders. This one doesn’t. These are eight films that ask something of the viewer: patience, discomfort, and a willingness to sit with silence and pay it back tenfold. None of them are new exactly, but none of them have aged either, which is the only test that matters.
Captain Fantastic (2016)
Matt Ross’s film follows a father raising six children off-grid in the Pacific Northwest, training them in survivalism, philosophy, and physical endurance instead of sending them to school. Viggo Mortensen plays Ben Cash with a conviction that never tips into caricature, and the film is smart enough to interrogate its own premise rather than simply celebrate it. When the family is forced back into mainstream American life after a death, the story becomes less about the righteousness of one parenting philosophy and more about the cost of certainty. It is funny, then devastating, then funny again, and it never resolves the argument it opens, which is exactly why it stays with you.
Incendies (2010)
Denis Villeneuve’s Incendies is the kind of film that recalibrates what you think a thriller can do with grief. Twin siblings in Montreal are sent by their late mother’s will to trace her past in an unnamed Middle Eastern country torn by civil war, and what they uncover unravels backward into one of the most devastating final-act revelations in contemporary cinema. Villeneuve resists sentimentality throughout; the horror is structural, historical, and inherited. It is not a film you watch twice lightly, but it is one that clarifies, brutally, how war reproduces itself through families long after the fighting stops.
Cure (1997)
Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Cure is often filed under J-horror, but that undersells it. A detective investigates a string of murders committed by ordinary people with no memory of the act, all connected to a drifter who seems to hypnotize victims into violence through nothing more than quiet, persistent questioning. The film’s power is in its restraint—long static shots, unresolved dread, and a refusal to explain itself fully. Kurosawa is less interested in a monster than in the idea that identity is thinner than we assume and that the right kind of pressure can make anyone’s sense of self collapse. It is one of the most unsettling films of the nineties precisely because it never raises its voice.
Children of Men (2006)
Alfonso Cuarón’s adaptation of P.D. James’s novel imagines a near future where two decades of global infertility have collapsed civil society into authoritarianism and despair, and one unexpected pregnancy becomes the only thing worth protecting. The technical achievement—those extended unbroken takes through combat zones and refugee camps—is often what gets discussed first, but the film’s real force is emotional: Clive Owen’s exhausted, reluctant hero is moving through a world that has simply stopped believing in the future. Watching it now, nearly two decades after release, its vision of border violence and refugee dehumanization feels less like prophecy and more like early reporting.
A Separation (2011)
Asghar Farhadi’s film begins with a couple’s divorce hearing and expands, with almost unbearable precision, into a study of class, faith, and the impossibility of clean moral judgment. Every character is right by their own logic and wrong by someone else’s, and Farhadi never lets the audience off the hook by picking a side for them. It remains one of the most disciplined pieces of screenwriting of the past fifteen years—nothing is wasted, and every small lie compounds into consequence.
The Handmaiden (2016)
Park Chan-wook’s adaptation of Sarah Waters’s Fingersmith, relocated to Japanese-occupied Korea, is a con-artist thriller, an erotic drama, and a colonial critique all folded into one lush, structurally audacious film. It tells the same span of events from multiple perspectives, each retelling recontextualizing what came before, until the story becomes as much about who gets to narrate as about what happened. It’s also simply gorgeous to look at, which makes its darker undercurrents—about ownership, performance, and women written by men for men—land harder.
Timbuktu (2014)
Abderrahmane Sissako’s film, set during the 2012 jihadist occupation of northern Mali, refuses the visual language typically used for stories like this. There is no spectacle of violence here; instead, Sissako shows daily life continuing, absurdly and heartbreakingly, under occupation—a football match played without a ball because the sport has been banned and a musician punished for singing. The restraint is the argument. It is one of the few films about extremism that treats its subjects as full people first.
Winter Sleep (2014)
Nuri Bilge Ceylan’s three-hour drama, set in a hotel carved into the rock of Cappadocia, is built almost entirely from conversation—long, corrosive arguments between a former actor turned landlord and his younger wife, his sister, and his tenants. It sounds punishing on paper and instead becomes riveting, because Ceylan understands that the most dangerous violence in a marriage or a family is rarely physical. It rewards the kind of patience most films no longer ask for and repays it completely.
Taken together, these eight films share very little in setting or genre. What they share is a refusal to simplify. Each trusts its audience to sit with ambiguity rather than resolve it for them, which is probably why none of them are comfortable and all of them are worth the two hours.

item.description:
The news that had been circulating as a rumour has now been confirmed: Lionel Messi’s father, Jorge Messi, has died at the age of 68.

Newell’s Old Boys, Messi’s first club, confirmed his death in a statement on social media.

Argentine media outlets Olé and La Nación have also confirmed the news of Jorge Messi’s death.

In a statement, Newell’s Old Boys said that Jorge Messi died in the city of Rosario at the age of 68.

“Club Atlético Newell’s Old Boys expresses its deepest condolences on the death of Jorge Messi,” the club said.

Messi broke down in tears after scoring against Algeria in Argentina’s opening match of the 2026 World Cup. After scoring a hat-trick, Messi told reporters that he was going through a difficult personal period.

A few days later, the Messi family said in a statement that the elder Messi was under medical supervision and that his condition was improving.

item.title: Bangladesh HP beat Malaysia by 89 runs
item.description:
The victory came by a convincing margin, but Bangladesh High Performance (HP) team may still have been left frustrated with their batting. They scored 158 runs in 20 overs against the Malaysia national team, with several batters giving away their wickets after playing poor shots.

The bowlers then made up for the batting shortcomings, dismissing Malaysia for just 69 runs as Bangladesh HP secured an 89-run victory.

Sent in to bat after losing the toss in Mirpur, Bangladesh made a poor start. Opener Jisan Alam faced seven balls without scoring. Under pressure after playing a string of dot balls, he attempted to hit a delivery from Arif Ullah that was well outside off stump but only managed to offer a catch inside the 30-yard circle.

His opening partner, Jowad Abrar, was far more aggressive. He struck three fours and a six before being dismissed for 28 off 18 balls.

The next three batters—Ariful Islam (15 off 12), Sabbir Rahman (14 off 12) and Pritom Kumar (4 off 7)—failed to build substantial innings.

Bangladesh’s biggest partnership came for the sixth wicket, with Mehrob Hasan and Abdul Gaffar adding 53 runs. They were the only two Bangladesh batters to score more than 30. Mehrob made 40 off 22 balls, including three fours and two sixes, while Abdul Gaffar scored 32 off 26.

However, after their dismissals, Bangladesh lost its final five wickets for 32 runs. Still, the total of 158 proved more than enough.

Malaysia’s batters struggled against Bangladesh’s bowling attack and never came close to mounting a serious challenge.

Ahmed Aqil Wahed was Malaysia’s top scorer, making 29 off 25 balls. Only two other batters reached double figures: Mohammad Amir scored 15 off 22 balls, while Vijay Unni made 14 off 15.

Malaysia were bowled out for 69 in just 16 overs.

For Bangladesh, Mohammad Rubel and Rakibul Hasan took two wickets each, while Abu Haider, Abdul Gaffar, Mehrob and Mrityunjoy Chowdhury claimed one wicket apiece.

item.title: PM: Fascism beneficiaries actively working to destabilise energy sector
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday said the beneficiaries of fascism remained active in the state, politics, governance and administration, and out to destabilise the country’s power and energy sector by spreading misleading information and creating confusion.
“Those who are benefited from fascism are not sitting idle. This group is quite active to destabilise the country’s energy and power sector in various ways. They were spreading misleading information about the sector,” he said.
The prime minister made the remarks while addressing a doctors’ rally organised on the occasion of the 37th founding anniversary of the Doctors Association of Bangladesh (DAB) at the LD Hall of the National Parliament complex on Saturday morning.
Tarique Rahman said previous governments’ unplanned projects and decisions had placed the country’s power and energy sector at risk, and the present government was working to protect the country and its people from its consequences.
“The government is not denying that people are currently facing crises of electricity, gas and fuel. But the country, its people and the government are now paying for those unplanned schemes to provide special benefits to certain quarters,” he noted.
The prime minister said plans are being formulated to gradually bring people out of the crises of gas, electricity and fuel.
Earlier, the prime minister and Dr Zubaida Rahman planted saplings of neem and arjun trees on the premises of the LD Hall of the National Parliament Bhaban.
They later formally inaugurated the doctors’ rally by hoisting the national and party flags and releasing balloons and pigeons.
DAB leaders and doctors from different parts of the country attended the gathering. DAB President Professor Dr Harun Al Rashid presided over the rally.
BNP Secretary General and LGRD and Cooperatives Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, Social Welfare Minister Abu Zafar Md. Zahid Hossain, Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain and DAB Secretary General Dr Md Zahirul Islam Shakil, among others, addressed the programme.
Citing a quote attributed to American inventor and businessman Thomas Alva Edison, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said future doctors would not prescribe medicines alone, but would educate patients about physical exercise, balanced diets and the causes and means of preventing diseases.
“The present government’s health policy is closely aligned with this approach,” he said, adding, “The present government believes in the principle that prevention is better than cure. Instead of seeking treatment after a disease develops, we should take necessary precautions beforehand to prevent it from occurring.”
The prime minister said the government had decided to recruit 100,000 new health workers across the country to raise public awareness about primary healthcare. “Doctors must take the lead in providing proper training to those health workers,” he said.
He said, “I believe that in a democratic state, where political decisions influence almost every aspect of life, it is not unreasonable for students, teachers and professionals to remain politically organised or politically aware according to their respective ideologies.”
Addressing the doctors, the prime minister said a number of proposals had been placed on their behalf to make the country’s health system and medical services more effective and people-oriented.
The proposals included recruiting 5,000 doctors through a special BCS examination within the shortest possible time; raising the age limit for entry into government service for doctors from 32 to 34 years; and increasing the retirement age of doctors from 61 to 65 years.
Other proposals included enacting a timely Health Services Protection Act to ensure the safety of both doctors and patients, introducing special allowances and incentives for doctors working at upazila and remote areas, formulating a specific and equitable pay structure for more than 100,000 doctors working in the private sector, and establishing specialised hospitals at divisional, district and upazila levels instead of concentrating such facilities in the capital.

Youth participation key to Bangladesh’s future, speakers say
item.description:
Young people must have a meaningful role in Bangladesh’s political, economic and social transformation if the aspirations of the July uprising are to translate into lasting change, speakers said at a webinar on Saturday.
The remarks came at the eighth episode of the Power and Participation Research Centre’s (PPRC) “Ajker Agenda” webinar, which focused on the aspirations, capabilities and challenges facing the country’s youth amid calls for political renewal, economic opportunity and social reform.
Tajnuva Jabeen, an organizer of the National Organizing Committee of Alternatives, said the July uprising had renewed political interest among young people and created an opportunity to challenge the stigma surrounding youth participation in politics.
“July reawakened something powerful — political interest among the youth,” she said, stressing the need to encourage professionals, including doctors, engineers and bankers, to enter politics.
She said a decentralized political system would be essential to building a better Bangladesh over the next 10 to 15 years.
Sakib Hossain, CEO of Fashol, highlighted the technology and information gaps affecting Bangladesh’s agriculture sector, particularly farmers’ dependence on intermediaries and uncertainty over access to markets.
Drawing on his experience of founding Fashol in 2019, he said young entrepreneurs could use technology to address long-standing problems in the agricultural sector.
“As a young entrepreneur, I saw technology transforming every industry except the one that feeds our nation,” he said, adding that youth-led innovation could help address gaps that previous generations had been unable to close.
Agri-entrepreneur and content creator Umma Kulsum Popi said agriculture remains one of Bangladesh’s most promising sectors, despite many young people viewing farming as a low-income and low-status profession.
“Ninety percent of our youth avoid farming, chasing careers with more income and respect,” she said, arguing that Bangladesh’s fertile soil could provide young people with opportunities to build sustainable livelihoods.
Daw Sing Nue Marma, team lead of TONGDAINGNEY, highlighted the role of youth networks and technology-supported education in the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
She said young people could help overcome language and geographic barriers and take education to communities through non-formal and nature-based approaches.
“Education needs to be reoriented to foster creativity, nurture values and expose young people to real-life issues,” she said.
Advocate Khalequzzaman said meaningful institutional change would require reforming the legal and administrative foundations of the state, including laws inherited from the colonial era.
He also criticized what he described as setbacks to judicial reform, saying a new generation of political leaders was needed to carry forward the push for systemic change.
Munim Mubashshir said the period following July 2024 had exposed a gap between young people’s contributions to the uprising and their participation in subsequent decision-making.
“So many young people who bled for July had the vision and ability to help rebuild this nation, but were never given a seat at the table,” he said.
He called for greater inclusion of young people in shaping the country’s future, saying their sacrifices should be followed by meaningful participation in national affairs.
Summing up the discussion, PPRC Chairman and session moderator Hossain Zillur Rahman said the desire for change that emerged from July was one of Bangladesh’s greatest strengths.
But turning that aspiration into lasting reform would require action across institutional spaces, from grassroots initiatives to broader structural reforms, he said.
“Young people are wide awake to this desire for change,” Hossain Zillur said. “The real question is whether we’re giving them the right environment and right opportunities to contribute.”

item.title: Police restrict Alia Madrasa access amid student hostel dispute
item.description:
Police restricted access to the road leading to Dhaka’s Madrasa-e-Alia (Alia Madrasa) near the Bakshibazar intersection for around two hours on Saturday amid tensions over access to the madrasa hostel, with Islami Chhatra Shibir alleging that students have been prevented from entering the dormitory since August 6.
The road was barricaded shortly after noon and remained restricted until around 2pm, preventing vehicles from entering the madrasa premises through that route. Vehicles leaving the area, however, faced no obstruction.
After the barricade was removed, police personnel remained stationed near the madrasa dormitory until around 6pm.
An assistant deputy commissioner of Lalbagh Division of Dhaka Metropolitan Police told Dhaka Tribune that no formal barricade had been imposed at the intersection.
He said traffic movement had instead been briefly controlled on one side of the road, while the other side remained fully open. The restriction lasted roughly one to one-and-a-half hours, from around 1pm to 2:30pm, as madrasa authorities invited student representatives for talks with the principal.
The officer, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said no notable incident took place at the madrasa on Saturday.
The development came amid allegations by Abdul Alim, president of the Islami Chhatra Shibir unit at the madrasa, that students have been unable to enter the hostel for the past three days.
Alim alleged that students trying to enter the hostel—including both Shibir activists and general students—were beaten and had their phones snatched by Chhatra Dal activists between August 6 and 8.
He claimed around six students had been beaten and said no students, whether affiliated with Shibir or not, had been able to enter the hostel during the period.
Alim further alleged that outsiders affiliated with Chhatra Dal and Jubo Dal had entered the dormitory carrying weapons.
He said there was no separate incident at the madrasa on Saturday.
The allegations could not be independently verified immediately.

item.title: Madhupur pineapple gaining popularity across country
item.description:
Pineapples produced at Madhupur in Tangail are gaining popularity across the country due to their distinctive taste and quality.
The red-soil terrain, climate and natural conditions of Madhupur are considered ideal for pineapple cultivation. The fruit has a long history in the region and has become an important source of income for local farmers.
The pineapple-growing season is now at its peak. Markets remain busy as traders collect the fruit and send it to different parts of the country. Depending on size and quality, pineapples are currently selling for Tk15-Tk50 each.
Farmers say prices largely depend on weather conditions. Excessive rainfall, adverse weather and natural disasters can reduce yields and cause prices to fall. They believe greater investment in pineapple processing, cold storage and value-added products could ensure fair prices for growers.
They also say measures to process pineapples and export them could open new opportunities, allowing them to receive better prices while creating demand for processed pineapple products in international markets.
Madhupur pineapple received Geographical Indication (GI) recognition on September 24, 2024, further strengthening its identity and market value.
The Jalchhobi market in Madhupur is considered one of the country's largest pineapple trading hubs. Markets at Mohat and Garob are also major centres. Wholesalers arrive from Mymensingh, Jamalpur, Kishoreganj, Sherpur, Dhaka, Sylhet, Rajshahi, Kushtia, Barisal and Gazipur to purchase the fruit.
According to the Department of Agricultural Extension, pineapple cultivation covers 7,573 hectares across the district this season, with production estimated at 287,182 tonnes. Of this, 6,943 hectares are in Madhupur, producing around 258,132 tonnes.
Farmer Sanwar Hossain said he cultivated pineapples on two acres without using chemicals and was selling large fruits for Tk30-Tk60 each.
Another farmer, Kabil Uddin, said it costs around Tk12 to produce a pineapple, making the crop profitable when market prices remain favourable.
Madhupur Upazila Agriculture Officer Rabiul Al Rana said the demand for the region's pineapples remains high nationwide because of their taste and quality. He expects yields of up to 35 tonnes per hectare this year.
Madhupur Upazila Executive Officer Jubaer Hossain said establishing pineapple-based industries and expanding exports could significantly benefit farmers.
Ashiq Parvez, deputy director of the district agricultural extension office, said a proposal has been sent to the ministry on safe production, proper marketing and ways to access international markets for Madhupur pineapples.

item.title: River erosion takes serious turn in Jamalpur
item.description:
Hundreds of riverside residents in Islampur upazila of Jamalpur are facing growing uncertainty as severe erosion along the Dashani River, a distributary of the Brahmaputra, continues to swallow homes, cropland, roads and other rural infrastructure.
The strong current has accelerated riverbank erosion in recent days, forcing many families to live in fear of losing their homes. A local market and an educational institution have also come under imminent threat as the river continues to devour the embankment.
A visit to the affected villages found residents living in constant anxiety as deep cracks have appeared along the riverbank, raising fears that large sections of land could collapse into the river at any time. Productive farmland—the primary source of income for many households—is disappearing day by day.
Farmer Rois Uddin said most of his agricultural land, along with his standing jute crop, had already been washed away. "I own only a few bighas of land, and most of it has been lost to the river. Now my house is also at risk. I don't know where my family and I will find shelter," he said.
Swarna Begum, the elderly widow of late Sharafat Ali, said the worsening erosion has left her unable to sleep at night. "I have nowhere to go. My husband is no longer alive, and I live in constant fear with my children," she said.
Local schoolteacher Md. Belayet Hossain warned that if the erosion continues unchecked, nearby homes, educational institutions and the local market could all be swallowed by the river. "Immediate protective measures are essential. Otherwise, the damage will be irreversible," he said.
Residents, including Md. Sekandar Ali, Shafizal Haque and Sabbir Wahed, said the Dashani River causes extensive erosion every monsoon, yet no permanent riverbank protection has been implemented. As a result, new areas are being lost to the river each year.
The Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) said the administration has inspected the affected areas and informed the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) about the situation.
Nakibuzzaman, Executive Engineer of the Jamalpur BWDB, said officials are closely monitoring the erosion and have reported the situation to higher authorities. "Necessary emergency measures will be taken as soon as we receive directives," he said.
Residents have called for the immediate placement of geo-bags at vulnerable points to slow the erosion, warning that without urgent intervention, many more families could lose their homes and farmland during the ongoing monsoon season. They also urged the government to undertake a permanent riverbank protection project to safeguard the area from recurring erosion.

item.title: US Senate confirms Trump’s ex-lawyer as attorney general
item.description:
The US Senate confirmed President Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer Todd Blanche as attorney general early Saturday after Republican lawmakers shrugged off Democratic concerns over politicization of the Department of Justice.
Blanche, who has already been serving as the top US law enforcement officer in an acting capacity, represented Trump as his private attorney in several criminal trials before entering government.
The Senate, which Republicans narrowly control, confirmed him by 50 votes to 49. Republican senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski joined the Democrats in voting no, underlining the political sensitivity over the nomination.
Blanche said he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice.”
“I am grateful to the Senate for staying late to complete this process. To the dedicated public servants of the Department of Justice, thank you for your work each day to uphold the law and keep our country safe,” Blanche wrote on X.
Trump, who has upended US political norms by seeking to bring nominally independent government agencies under his increasingly direct control, calls Blanche a “star.”
Democrats opposed Blanche from the beginning, accusing Trump of turning the Department of Justice into a political weapon.
“The attorney general is supposed to be the people’s lawyer,” Senator Dick Durbin, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said on Tuesday.
“Mr Blanche continues to operate as the president’s personal lawyer, treating the Justice Department like a law firm serving one client -- the president.”
There were doubts over whether the White House could persuade a handful of Republican holdouts, without whom even the narrow confirmation would have been impossible.
The main sticking point was an attempt to establish a $1.8 billion fund for what Trump calls victims of politicized prosecutions, likely including the rioters who stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021 in an attempted insurrection to prevent Joe Biden from being certified as president, after he had defeated Trump in the 2020 election.
The other main issue was an extraordinary proposal granting immunity to Trump from tax audits. Blanche ultimately defused the internal party opposition with a written order over the weekend scrapping the so-called political “anti-weaponization fund” and saying that the audit immunity agreement with Trump, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization would only apply “retroactively” to the past tax years and not future filings.
Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since Trump fired Pam Bondi, another political loyalist, in April.
Since then, he has been closely tied to what Democrats dub a Trump “retribution” campaign against the 80-year-old president’s opponents.
Blanche has also come in for criticism from victims of Jeffrey Epstein over the handling of the release of investigative files about the convicted sex offender, a one-time close friend of Trump.
Prior to joining the Department of Justice, Blanche represented Trump in his New York trial over alleged “hush money” paid to porn star Stormy Daniels.
He was also on the legal defense team in two federal cases brought against Trump by special counsel Jack Smith -- for allegedly mishandling classified documents after leaving the White House, and for seeking to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.
Both cases were dropped after Trump won the 2024 election.

Torrential rain, waterlogging cause extensive damage to Aush paddy in Narail
item.description:
Prolonged rainfall and persistent waterlogging have caused extensive damage to Aush paddy in large areas of Narail district, leaving hundreds of farmers facing heavy financial losses.
Local farmers blamed the situation on blocked natural drainage routes, unplanned fish enclosures and the filling up of canals and drainage channels due to poor maintenance.
They fear the total financial losses from the crop damage will run into several crores of taka.
During a visit to several low-lying areas, including Amadar, Andharkota and Kuchiabari bills in Lohagara upazila, fields were found submerged under chest-deep water.
Instead of ripening paddy, the fields were covered with water lilies and other aquatic weeds, while groups of ducks were seen roaming through the waterlogged farmland.
Affected farmers said the low-lying lands are particularly suitable for the local water-tolerant variety of Aush paddy known as “Ratul Aush.” The variety can grow rapidly as water levels rise.
Farmers had expanded cultivation of the variety this year after obtaining good yields and prices in previous years amid moderate rainfall.
Apart from Lakshmipasha, Ratul Aush was cultivated in more than 50 bills across different unions of the district, including Bangram, Naldhi, Kotakol, Kalabaria, Baiashona, Pohardanga, Khashial, Maijpara and Sekhati.
However, record rainfall that began in mid-July suddenly inundated the low-lying farmland.
Farmers said water remained trapped for a prolonged period because unplanned fish enclosures blocked drainage routes, eventually causing the submerged paddy plants to rot.
The farmers demanded immediate removal of illegal fish enclosures, restoration of blocked canals and drains and re-excavation of connecting canals linked to rivers to improve water drainage.
This year, some 9,107 hectares of land have been brought under Aush paddy cultivation, according to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) in Narail.
Although officials have estimated the crop damage to be limited, farmers strongly disputed the assessment.
They said some paddy in relatively higher areas survived, but most of the crops in low-lying areas had rotted, resulting in losses worth several crores of taka.
Muhammad Arifur Rahman, deputy director of the Narail Department of Agricultural Extension, said the agriculture department was coordinating with other relevant government agencies to restore drainage systems and recover canals that have been filled in or disappeared.
“Permanent waterlogging in the low-lying water body areas has become a major threat to agricultural activities,” he said.

46 maunds of hilsa caught in a single net, sold for nearly Tk 5m
item.description:
A fishing trawler has caught 46 maunds of hilsa in a single net in the Bay of Bengal near Kuakata in Patuakhali.

The fish were sold at Mahipur Fishery Port on Friday for approximately Tk 4.85 million (Tk 48.5 lakh).

The unusually large catch has brought renewed excitement among fishermen in the coastal area after a prolonged period of poor catches.

Alamgir Majhi, the owner of the fishing trawler FB Junaid, was on board when the fish were caught. He said the trawler caught 46 maunds of hilsa on Thursday near the last buoy of Payra Sea Port.

The trawler, loaded with hilsa, reached Mahipur Fishery Port at noon on Friday. The fish were then sold through an auction at a wholesale fish outlet called Manowara Fish.

“It has been nearly five years since I got such a large consignment of hilsa at once. This is great news. Catching 2,200 hilsa in a single net is no small thing. We have suffered losses for a long time, and with such a big catch, we hope to recover some of those losses, ” said Alamgir Hossain, owner of FB Junaid.

Sagir Akon, manager of Manowara Fish, said 24 maunds of the catch consisted of hilsa weighing 1kg or more. They bought those fish at Tk 115,000 per maund, equivalent to Tk 2,875 per kg. The 24 maunds therefore cost Tk 2.76 million.

The remaining 22 maunds consisted of hilsa weighing between 800 and 900 grams. Those were purchased at Tk 95,000 per maund, or Tk 2,375 per kg, bringing the total cost to Tk 2.09 million.

The entire 46-maund catch was therefore purchased for Tk 4.85 million.
Sagir Akon said hilsa prices this year were significantly higher than last year.

“Hilsa prices are very high in the market, so the fishermen who caught these 46 maunds received a good price,” he said.

Apu Saha, senior fisheries officer, Kalapara upazila, said,  “There has been a shortage of hilsa in the sea for quite some time. However, fishermen are still catching varying amounts of hilsa. If the rainfall continues, the catch is likely to increase further.”

Hilsa catches in the sea have declined compared with previous years, with overall production also falling. This has put pressure on fishermen’s livelihoods.

Mohammad Bakhtiar Rahman, a research assistant with the Healthy Ocean project implemented by WCS and WorldFish with funding from the Blue Action Fund, described the large catch as encouraging news for fishermen.

According to Bakhtiar, the catch could give hope to fishermen who spend days and nights at sea. However, he cautioned that such a large catch in a single day should not be considered an indicator of an overall abundance of hilsa.

He said the situation could be properly assessed later through continued monitoring and scientific data on fish availability.

He also stressed that maintaining the positive trend would require greater awareness among fishermen, avoiding fishing during the breeding season and ensuring the continued implementation of conservation measures.

Apu Saha, senior fisheries officer of Kalapara upazila, told Prothom Alo that hilsa availability in the sea had been declining for some time. However, fishermen were still catching hilsa in varying quantities.

“If the rainfall continues, more hilsa will be caught,” he said. “The greater the volume of hilsa caught, the more fishermen, fish traders and others involved in the hilsa trade will benefit.”

item.title: Iran says deal on Strait of Hormuz is close but not enough to open the waterway
item.description:
SAUDI ARAMCO-RESULTS/

Iran said on Saturday that a deal with Oman on control of the Strait of Hormuz was close but would not be enough to free up the waterway, and the United Arab Emirates said Iran had hit another ship there.

Agreement between Iran and Oman over the strait is seen as vital to a wider deal to end the war that began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February and led to Tehran establishing a chokehold over the major energy export route.

A US official, who declined to be identified, had said on Friday that Washington anticipated an agreement soon between Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, so that normal oil traffic could resume.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Iran and Oman were "very close" to agreement on a new shipping route through the strait but that reopening it depended on other conditions, including US compensation to Iran.

The secretary of Iran's top national security body, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, listed other demands including ending US threats against Iran, stopping aggression against Iran and its Lebanese, Palestinian, Yemeni and Iraqi allies, lifting a blockade and sanctions on Iran and freeing Iranian assets.

US hopeful Hormuz strait deal will be done “today or tomorrow”

Oman Reports Positive Negotiations, Condemns Ship Attacks

Oman condemned what it described as repeated attacks on vessels while transiting the strait, without assigning blame, and said that negotiations with Iran on arrangements for shipping through Hormuz were "positive and constructive".

"Oman stresses the importance of avoiding any actions that could affect these negotiations and the progress achieved in a manner that takes into account the interests of all parties," the foreign ministry said.

Araqchi said the previous shipping traffic separation scheme through the strait was no longer acceptable to Tehran and that Iran was discussing a temporary route with Oman while technical and legal issues surrounding a permanent route were resolved.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement.

"There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war," Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.

Iran has responded to the US attacks by targeting US bases in Gulf states and Jordan as well as striking shipping in the narrow strait, which carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments before the war.

The UAE said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a carrier affiliated with its state oil company with a missile as it transited the Strait of Hormuz, with no injuries reported, in the latest escalation in attacks on shipping there. The UK maritime trade monitor UKMTO said a vessel had caught fire after being hit by an unknown projectile but the fire was put out and there was no reported environmental impact.

US used “virtually all” of its long-range missiles during Iran war

There was no immediate comment from Iranian authorities.

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has repeatedly signaled that a deal to open the strait could be close, only to have Iran deny that talks are under way. It was unclear whether the latest flurry of negotiations would yield a more lasting arrangement.

"Once the deal is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports," the US official told Reuters on Friday. US actions would be tied to Iran's implementation of its commitments, he said.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who have targeted the ships, also said on Saturday that reopening the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington accepting Iran's conditions and was not related to the Iran-Oman negotiations.

"Whenever the United States accepts Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will certainly be reopened," said Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi, according to Iran's Tasnim news agency.

Sources Said This Week a Deal Would Give Iran Some Control

A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to help end five months of war between Iran and the US would give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the strait, a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran.

US officials have repeatedly said they would never agree to Iran controlling access to the world's most important trade route for energy supplies. It was not clear whether they had sought to change the parameters of the deal.

Iran has used the hostilities to justify charging a toll on oil tankers. That, and the firing on ships that attempt to cross the strait without its permission, has badly disrupted global shipments, causing energy prices to surge and fueling inflation.

item.title: Tarique Rahman was tortured at JIC during 1/11: ICT chief prosecutor
item.description:
Chief Prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) Md Aminul Islam today, Saturday said witnesses in different cases have testified that incumbent Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was tortured at the Joint Interrogation Cell (JIC) at the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI) headquarters in Dhaka during the 1/11 period.

"The JIC that we visited today was the place where the Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was brought to one of its rooms during the 1/11 period. We have also found information through the accounts of various witnesses during our investigation that he was subjected to torture there. These findings will be reflected in the trials in due course," he said while talking to newsmen at the DGFI headquarters after inspecting the JIC this noon.

Terming today's visit as part of the trial proceedings, the chief prosecutor said, people were brought to this facility, detained and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.

"It later became known as 'Aynaghar'. Detainees were held there in inhumane conditions for days, months and even years. We were able to get some sense of the brutality they endured through today's visit," he added.

Md Aminul Islam said they will urge the government to ensure that no TFI (Task Force for Interrogation) cell, JIC or so-called 'Aynaghar' is ever established again in Bangladesh in the future.

"If any citizen of the country commits a crime, he or she must be brought under the law and made to face trial. But no citizen should ever become a victim of any extrajudicial killing. No one should be subjected to unnecessary harassment by any law enforcement agency. No one should be detained and subjected to harassment in custody for days or months," he further said.

Led by ICT-1 Chairman Justice Golam Mortuza Mazumder, the delegation that inspected the JIC included Justice Shafiul Alam Mahmud and Justice Mohitul Haque Enam Chowdhury, Daily Manabzamin Editor Matiur Rahman Chowdhury, Supreme Court Reporters Forum General Secretary Mehedi Hasan Dalim, its Executive Committee Member Mazharul Hoque Manna, and Law Reporters Forum President Md Yasin, among others.

item.title: Why intellectuals become collaborators of autocracy
item.description:
Altaf Hossain was originally from Sylhet but was a staunch supporter of Pakistan. During the regime of military dictator Ayub Khan, his responsibility as the editor of the Dawn newspaper was to turn Bengalis into Pakistanis and Muslims. He was so successful in this task that Ayub gave him a place in his cabinet.

Altaf Hossain was not alone. Since the creation of Pakistan in 1947 and Bangladesh's independence in 1971, we have rarely experienced true democracy. Most of the time has passed under authoritarian regimes. During this long period, a section of Bengali intellectuals have stood by autocratic and semi-autocratic governments for one excuse or another. Some in the name of religion, some in the name of anti-Indianism, some in the name of the spirit of the liberation war, and some in the name of secularism and development have found justifications for siding with despotism.

Fall of Sheikh Hasina and lessons from history

We can also mention Syed Sajjad Hossain, who, despite witnessing the massacre of 1971, accepted it in the name of maintaining Pakistan's territorial integrity. Shortly after the Pakistani army launched a brutal attack on Dhaka University, he was rewarded by Pakistani authorities with the position of Vice-Chancellor of the same university. He was so loyal to Pakistan that he viewed the emergence of Bangladesh as the ''fall'' of East Pakistan.

As intellectuals, they forgot that their primary duty as intellectuals was not to befriend power but to relentlessly challenge the centres of power. They did the opposite. It's easy to protest against the enemy's injustice, but standing against one's own side's injustice is the true test of an intellectual's integrity. In this critical test, Awami intellectuals of Bangladesh have utterly failed.

There was no need for him to openly celebrate the genocide. He developed a narrative to uphold Pakistan's ideals, which portrayed the army as maintaining national unity and the Bengali resistance as an Indian-instigated separatism. This way, all the atrocities were obscured by ideology.

Constructing Consent

I'm not suggesting that Bengali intellectuals have a monopoly on constructing narratives in support of autocracy. Throughout history, there have always been groups of intellectuals eager to justify ruthless and diabolical regimes.

Antonio Gramsci and George Orwell have explained this concept very clearly and straightforwardly. What we now refer to as ''manufacturing consent'', riding on Noam Chomsky's shoulders, was first exposed by Gramsci in his Prison Notebooks. According to Gramsci, everyone is an intellectual, whether a bricklayer or a pen-professor, as we all use our intellect in some form of work.

However, there is a group among intellectuals whose job is to advocate for power using ladders of opinion, belief, or ideology. Without the narratives they construct, it would be impossible for dictatorships to survive. For Stalin, Hitler, Ayub, or Hasina, these intellectuals are as essential as fuel is to a car.

When the state is unable to fulfill its fundamental responsibilities

The autocrat's weapon is the gun. The intellectual's weapon is their pen and language. British journalist and author George Orwell demonstrated how a group of intellectuals could use everyday language to prove even the ruthless dictators like Stalin or Hitler as indispensable.

One function of political language is to prove truth as falsehood and falsehood as truth. This task is best accomplished by the country's prominent intellectuals. They are popular and have acceptance among ordinary citizens. So when such an intellectual takes up the pen for a corrupt king, whether they are a poet, journalist, or actor, people listen to them attentively and place their trust in their words. Their advocacy not only spares lies but also cold-blooded disappearances and murders.

When intellectuals become followers of autocracy

In Bangladesh, some intellectuals have turned into supporters of Awami authoritarianism while offering uncompromising support for the values of the Liberation War based on their ideological foundation. Civil rights are violated in the country, voting rights are taken away, and freedom of speech is restricted. Like everyone else, they too have witnessed these violations firsthand. The only difference is that they have considered these violations necessary for ideological reasons, singing praises or remaining silent in their support.

When it comes to the values of the Liberation War, these intellectuals have prioritised three things—preservation of the history of 1971, opposition to fundamentalism, and secularism. These are important values, but the spirit of the Liberation War is not limited to these principles or ideals. The rule of law, an independent judiciary, voting rights, freedom of speech, and an egalitarian society are also part of this spirit.

All of these values have been violated from the very beginning of the Awami era. In the last sixteen years of Hasina's rule, these violations have multiplied a hundredfold, turning into a full-fledged autocratic system. Yet, the blind eyes of the Awami intellectuals remain blind.

We have seen many intellectuals who are unwavering about the history and values of 1971. Yet, they have almost unconditionally supported Hasina's autocracy. When elections were held without votes, many of them argued that there is no alternative to Sheikh Hasina for Bangladesh. They considered siding with Hasina their duty. Some argued that there is no alternative to Hasina for maintaining secularism.

We saw in July 2024, when students and innocent people were being killed like birds at the hands of the security forces, almost every vice-chancellor of the country's major universities went to Ganabhaban to express their support for the measures taken by Prime Minister Hasina against the students and the public.

Many have privately acknowledged that democracy has been downgraded in Hasina's hands, or that the measures taken to stay in power are repressive. Yet, these conscientious intellectuals have considered Hasina and the Awami regime as the sole safeguards of the Liberation War. It's not that they were unaware of the contradiction involved. But after repeating the mantra for years, they themselves became lackeys of the autocracy.

The responsibility of intellectuals is not to befriend power

During the Soviet era, there were many intellectuals and devoted communists who, despite being aware of Stalin's autocratic rule, did not renounce their support for it. They believed there was no alternative to Stalin for the victory of the socialist revolution. One of them was Nikolai Bukharin. He was hung by the neck at Stalin's hands.

The famous German philosopher Martin Heidegger can also be mentioned. He believed in the superiority of the German nation and thought there was no alternative to Hitler to establish this superiority in the world.

The similarity between their arguments and propositions and the stance of Bangladeshi intellectuals in support of Hasina's dictatorship is striking. Bukharin knew that Stalin's hands were stained with the blood of innocent people; yet, he could not dissociate the revolution from the party, or the party from its leader.

Heidegger elevated Hitler from the position of an ordinary political ruler to a personification of Germany's historical destiny. Similarly, in Bangladesh, these intellectuals helped create a unified moral entity by merging secularism, the Awami League, and Sheikh Hasina.

As intellectuals, they forgot that their primary duty as intellectuals was not to befriend power but to relentlessly challenge the centres of power. They did the opposite. It's easy to protest against the enemy's injustice, but standing against one's own side's injustice is the true test of an intellectual's integrity. In this critical test, Awami intellectuals of Bangladesh have utterly failed.

#Hasan Ferdous is an essayist and columnist.

*Opinions expressed here are the author's own.

BNP leader dies of snakebite, family alleges antivenom was withheld
item.description:
A BNP leader died after being bitten by a snake in Galachipa upazila of Patuakhali on Saturday, with his family alleging that he was referred to Patuakhali without being administered antivenom at the local health complex.
The deceased was identified as Zakir Hossain Mridha, 45, son of Fazlul Karim Mridha of Kalikapur village in Galachipa Sadar Union. He was the general secretary of Ward No 1 BNP in the union.
The incident occurred around 7:30am when Jakir was having tea at home. A snake bit him on a toe of his left foot. After spotting the snake, he informed his wife and family members quickly took him to Galachipa Upazila Health Complex.
According to the hospital register, Zakir was admitted at around 7:45am. His family alleged that he was referred to Patuakhali without being given antivenom or adequate treatment.
His elder brother and former union parishad member, Abdul Awad Mridha, alleged that no treatment was provided at the hospital.
“My brother might have survived if he had been given antivenom. We demand a proper investigation into why he was referred without receiving antivenom or necessary treatment,” he said.
Ambulance driver Md Jewel said Zakir was conscious when they left for Patuakhali and that there was no delay on the way. However, doctors at a Patuakhali hospital declared him dead upon arrival.
Explaining the decision not to administer antivenom, attending physician Jannatul Naim Tanha said zakir was brought to the hospital in critical condition, with very high blood pressure and heart rate.
“Considering the possibility of a cardiac problem, we consulted senior physicians and decided not to administer antivenom before referring him to Patuakhali,” she said.
Galachipa Upazila Health and Family Planning Officer Md Mezbah Uddin said the health complex had 40 vials of antivenom in stock but it was not administered because Zakir had breathing difficulties, high blood pressure and was in critical condition.
“Based on his initial symptoms, it was not possible to determine whether he had been bitten by a venomous snake. After consulting a senior consultant, the attending physician decided to refer him to Patuakhali for better treatment,” he said.
Mezbah added that the hospital would investigate any complaint from the family and take necessary action if needed.
Meanwhile, Zakir’s family and local residents have demanded an investigation into whether antivenom was required, whether the doctors’ decision was appropriate given his condition and why the medicine was not administered.
Abdul Qaiyum, director of Animal Lovers of Patuakhali, claimed that Zakir had symptoms consistent with a venomous snakebite and should have been kept at the hospital for treatment rather than being referred elsewhere.
He said breathing difficulties and a sensation of the throat closing can be symptoms of venomous snakebite and argued that emergency supportive care should have been provided if the patient’s breathing was failing.

item.title: ‘Fish sanctuaries to be expanded in haors as govt moves to scrap leasing system’
item.description:
The government is taking steps to establish more fish sanctuaries in haors and wetlands to increase the breeding and production of native freshwater fish, Fisheries and Livestock and Agriculture Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid said on Saturday.
He also said initiatives are underway to replace the existing leasing system for water bodies with a new mechanism aimed at protecting the interests of local communities.
The minister made the remarks while talking to journalists after inspecting the venue of the inaugural ceremony of National Fisheries Week 2026 at Achmita George Institution Mini Stadium in Katiadi upazila of Kishoreganj.
He said Bangladesh once had abundant native fish in its haors, baors, rivers, canals and wetlands. However, the availability of freshwater fish has declined over time due to the use of pesticides and chemical fertilisers, destruction of fish habitats and the shrinking of natural sanctuaries.
To address the situation, the government plans to create safe habitats for fish in haors and wetlands, including large pits and deep water-bodies where fish can breed and be conserved, he said.
“If fish eggs and fry can be protected, fish production will naturally increase,” the minister said, adding that sanctuary-based conservation of native freshwater fish would be strengthened.
Asked about concerns over microplastics in fish, Aminur Rashid said it was not only a problem for Bangladesh but a global concern. Microplastics have also been detected in seawater and marine fish, he said.
Bangladesh will take necessary measures in line with international research and decisions on the issue, he said, adding that the Environment Ministry’s relevant initiatives would also be important.

item.title: Two-day secondary teacher training and digital learning program ends
item.description:
A two-day teacher training program for nearly 70 mathematics teachers and head teachers from 21 secondary schools across four upazilas in Panchagarh ended on Saturday.
Jointly organized by Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), SAJIDA Foundation, and Kazi Farms Group, the workshop titled "Khan Academy Bangladesh Masterclass" and the closing ceremony were held at Eco Mahananda Cottage in Tetulia and attended by participating secondary school teachers, head teachers, and senior government officials.
Participating mathematics teachers received hands-on practical training on using classroom technology to make math learning accessible and engaging through the 'Khan Academy Bangladesh' platform. Additionally, head teachers gained detailed insights into utilising the platform's monitoring dashboard to observe school-level progress and performance. Alongside training, technical repair support is being provided to ensure functional digital equipment across participating schools.
At the closing ceremony, Chief Guest Nahida Parvin, Deputy Director (Research & Innovation Section, DSHE), stated: "As a mathematics student and educator myself, I deeply understand the necessity of math. Math is a subject where one concept cannot be understood without grasping its prerequisites; therefore, learning with conceptual understanding is crucial."
She further noted: "The government and all stakeholders are committed to ensuring quality education. I extend special thanks to the organizers for bringing such innovative projects to remote areas like Panchagarh. Our primary objective should be to spread development to peripheral regions across the country, rather than focusing solely on Dhaka."
Azwa Nayeem, CEO of Khan Academy Bangladesh, delivered the welcome address. She expressed gratitude to head teachers, teachers, and government officials, stating: "The Khan Academy platform plays a highly effective role in creating tech-supported classrooms. We seek everyone's full cooperation so that students, teachers, and head teachers can seamlessly use this platform to achieve math proficiency." She also extended sincere thanks to Kazi Farms for providing financial support to run operations in Panchagarh.
Attending the event, Md. Shariful Islam, Head Teacher of Bhojonpur Dimukhi High School, expressed his determination to track student progress via the dashboard to elevate all students to the 'Mastered' or proficient level in math.
Kazi Zeeshan Hasan, Director of Kazi Farms Group, stated in his speech: "Alongside business, Kazi Farms aims to create a positive impact on society through education. As we have multiple business operations in Panchagarh, we are delighted to contribute to the expansion of quality education in this remote and peripheral region of the country."
Among others, Jeshan Ahmed, Research Officer (Planning & Development Division, DSHE), Khairul Anam Md. Aftabur Rahman Helali (District Education Officer, Panchagarh), Ramizah Ahmed (Manager, Partnership & Fundraising Unit, SAJIDA Foundation), Khandaker Ahmed Ali (General Manager, Kazi Farms Limited), Upazila Secondary Education Officers, and other local administrative officials were present at the event.
With financial and technical support from SAJIDA Foundation and Kazi Farms, and with approval from DSHE, 'Khan Academy Bangladesh' is currently running its operations across 100 secondary schools in 7 districts -- Dhaka, Cumilla, Narayanganj, Gazipur, Narsingdi, Chandpur, and Panchagarh.
